insights.claim: Review should mandate a light check that code runs and reproduces the main figure, with deeper audits optional.
Running code and verifying data should fall to a dedicated checker, not already-overloaded scientific reviewers.
Formal reproducibility checks set the minimum standard, while open preprint review is an unmeasured bonus.
Randomizing accepted papers to an added code check can measure errors that standard review lets through.
If review caught shaky code, fewer weak positive results would be published and cited disproportionately.
Whether public comments on preprints actually change the final published paper remains largely unstudied.
Comparing preprints that received substantive comments against matched uncommented ones can trace published changes to comments.
Public preprint comments may counter citation bias by prompting authors to cite overlooked null results.
Open preprint review becomes useful only when structured or invited, rather than an unread comment box.
Automated integrity flags on preprints should go privately to reviewers, never be displayed publicly.
Registered reports can work in ecology if Stage 1 protocols include contingencies for droughts or floods.
Long field seasons and messy data make ecology especially prone to analysis choices made after seeing data.
Positive findings are cited far more than comparable null studies, distorting what fields consider settled.
Citation gaps by result direction must be adjusted for venue and publication year before being attributed to bias.
Hiring by paper counts and citation bias toward positive results reinforce each other as a system-level incentive.
Manipulated images may partly explain why some highly cited positive results look unusually clean.
A clear null finding is worth publishing, consistent with the argument that null results deserve citation.
An image-duplication detector with documented validation metrics can be shared across research-integrity groups.
Gradient-based descriptors may catch contrast-adjusted reused images without inflating false positives.
Journals can screen every submission automatically for duplicated images, routing only flags to humans.
Automated image flags require blinded human confirmation before being counted as integrity problems.
Running the detector on preprint and published versions shows whether publicly flagged image problems get fixed.
Recomputing p-values from statistics parsed out of messy PDFs should initially flag only gross inconsistencies.
Papers with image problems may also tend to contain statistical reporting errors.

adjacent_ideas.claim: Statistical reporting inconsistencies may be more frequent in highly cited positive studies than in null ones.
Registered reports might narrow the citation gap between positive and null findings in ecology.
Automated statistical consistency checks could serve as the cheap mandatory tier of staged reproducibility review.
Public preprint commenters may catch different integrity problems than automated image and statistics screens do.
